blocks.content: The first four minutes of running are bad. Your body asks questions your brain doesn't have answers for yet — why are we doing this, when does it stop, is this actually helping anything — and the only way through is just to keep going until the questions stop.
Around minute five, something shifts. The noise gets quieter. And then I'm just looking.
That's the part I run for. Not the distance, not the fitness, though I know those matter. Just the few minutes where my head stops talking and I can actually see things.

The bakery on the corner runs their ovens overnight. By the time I hit the sidewalk the whole block is warm from it — not temperature warm, something else, the kind of warmth that's more about smell than air. I've tried to paint it twice. Both times I got the light right and lost everything else. There are things that don't translate and I'm still deciding if that bothers me.
I turned left at the corner and picked up the pace on the downhill.
I've run this route enough times that my legs know it without me. Which is the point, I think. Some things should just run themselves.
